item.title: Why Social Media Is Ruining Travel for the Rest of Us
item.description:
Social Media

Why Social Media Is Ruining Travel for the Rest of Us

How the places we visit reflect who we are and who we hope to become.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Viral tourism has produced mass conformity.
  • Our travel choices reflect aspects of our social environments, such as our peer groups and cultural rites.
  • Some people identify as a “traveler” rather than “tourist,” aiming to connect authentically with a new locale.
  • For these travelers, pursuing uncomfortable or unexpected travel experiences creates psychological richness.

There’s a growing consensus that Instagram and TikTok are ruining travel for the rest of us. Viral tourism has led to a crush of travelers in a small number of destinations. A 2019 survey found that 86 percent of people chose their travel destinations based on social media content posted by a friend, family member, or peer. This wave of mass conformity led TIME magazine to declare that “We Have All Become Travel Influencers. It’s Ruining the Planet.”

Source: Viral meme, original source unknown

The trend of influencers lining up to get the exact same photo has become so common that it’s produced an industry of parody. One of our personal favorites is “@Influencersinthewild,” which captures videos and images of influencers (or wannabe influencers) trying to take selfies in the cringiest fashion. Occasionally, a middle-aged dad will recreate his daughter’s social media poses to reveal the absurdity of the entire enterprise.

These trends have a deep social psychological foundation. Long before we ever board a flight, our travel choices serve as powerful signals of status, values, and the subtle identities we hope to project to the world. Where people travel, for example, is influenced by the fads and fashions of their peer groups—whether to emulate our friends or our favorite social media celebrity. Clifford Lewis and colleagues interviewed young Australians about their travel choices and found that destinations can serve as “symbolic brands” that “satisfy needs…for self-expression and prestige.”

One interviewee said, “…You don’t find many people who are our age who haven’t gone to Europe [or] aren’t planning to go to Europe. If they say they don’t want to do it, you’re like, why?” Another noted, “It’s an achievement like you put it up on Facebook and then everyone can see it.”

At other times, people’s destinations reflect a desire to connect with deeper aspects of their ethnic, cultural, or religious identities. They might wish to visit an ancestral homeland or undertake a pilgrimage to a hallowed religious site, steeped in ancient meaning.

Source: Power of Us & Hannah Karsting

Travel is frequently a rite of passage, a transition between life stages. Graduates backpack around Asia, tour European cities, or drive across America to mark the transformation from carefree student life to the more serious identities of adulthood and career. Undertaking one of the most dramatic rites of passage, some Amish youths go on the Rumspringa, during which they leave their closely knit sect to spend a year or two in the secular world before deciding whether to return to the Amish community for life. (For a fascinating documentary about Rumspringa, watch Devil’s Playground.)

Even a more modest annual vacation is an identity-involving event. When we turn on our “out of office” message and leave our pet in the care of a friend, it is not just a chance to escape the routines and hassles of normal life. It’s an opportunity to briefly try on different ways of being—different possible selves. As we tour museums and art galleries, we often say, “We should do this sort of thing more often.” When we eat in interesting restaurants or try new cuisines, we re-envision ourselves as foodies.

Many of us also take pains to project the right kind of identity when we’re away from home. We might, for example, be eager not to be classified as mere tourists—that category of visitors wielding selfie sticks and despised by locals. And for good reason. Residents in Barcelona and Mallorca, Spain, have taken to attacking tourists with water guns to protest the surge of overtourism ruining the culture of the city and driving up prices.

Instead, many of us want to be seen as travelers, worldly people in search of authentic food, real culture—the genuine experience. Folks who can blend into the local culture without disturbing the residents or embarrassing ourselves.

Source: QuotesFancy

After analyzing blogs and online writing by people who self-identified as travelers rather than tourists, Lara Weeks concluded, “‘Traveling’ is often taken for granted as being an objectively better way of interacting cross-culturally, on the presumption that it does not cause the same problems as mass tourism.” Wrote one blogger:

"I am not a tourist, I am a traveler and the difference between the two is this: one serves to suck energy, the other to share and to learn with cultures and experiences."

It is easy to understand why people prefer to see themselves as travelers rather than tourists. It is a higher status identity. It is distinctive from the hordes of people crowding the Trevi Fountain or Taj Mahal, yet bonds you to a group of similarly-minded others. It feels more meaningful.

Importantly, people who embrace a “traveler” identity often seek off-the-beaten-path experiences that foster psychological richness—an essential yet often overlooked dimension of a good life. Brought on by interesting, perspective-shifting encounters, psychologically rich experiences are not necessarily comfortable or pleasant. The pursuit of these experiences may explain the core divide between tourists and travelers: as one of the travel bloggers (mentioned above) noted, “The traveler goes to bed exhausted, while the tourist has every comfort perfectly planned.” Another wrote: “I want to see it all. And, hopefully, survive.”

These quotes capture the notion that travel is not just travel. Like everything else, it’s loaded with psychological meaning. It can expand our sense of who we are or who we could be. It can bridge life’s transitions. It can connect us to our histories or be employed as a signal that we belong or an indicator of status. Far from home, professional travelers and vacationers alike work to project certain kinds of identities.

So, before you embark on your next vacation, think carefully about whether you want to be a tourist or a traveler.

item.title: Moral Realism and the Persistence of Ethical Myths
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Moral Realism and the Persistence of Ethical Myths

Why the belief in objective morality endures despite scientific progress.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Moral realism persists due to deep-seated human intuitions, not objective facts.
  • Moral language fuels culture wars by turning subjective values into dogmatic conflicts.
  • Human psychology is hard-wired for dogmatism, impeding the acceptance of moral nihilism.
The Myth of Morality
Source: Image created with Chat-GPT

Moral realism is the view that there are moral facts, that there are objective moral properties out there in the world.

But there are not.

Notions like ‘rights’, ‘wrongs’, and ‘duties’ are leftovers from a pre-scientific age in which dogma and myths ruled over evidence and reason. And much like unicorns, gods, and other fairy tales, they should be consigned to hell.

Despite the pride we take from human scientific and technological advancements, our minds, our brains are as much obstacles to these achievements as they are its cause. Humans are largely irrational and addicted to their own intuitions, which we had to overcome in order to develop modern science.

Of course, even when it comes to science, we have hardly overcome this psychology. The rise of anti-scientific sentiments is not a reflection of the realization of flaws of science, as some conspiracy theorists may proudly proclaim, but simply a reflection of our poorly designed primate brains (from the perspective of finding out truths about the world).

But when it comes to morals, our thinking has barely changed from our ancestors. The dogma of moral realism firmly remains part of much of our modern culture. This is emphasised perhaps nowhere more strongly than in today’s culture wars, which have turned differences in subjective values into the death of reason itself. For we now know quite well that participation in political causes tends to diminish your capacities as a reasoner. Much like rooting for a particular team in sports can turn one into an irrational hooligan.

The great Harvard psychologist Joshua David Greene wrote a PhD thesis, not in psychology, but in philosophy. Under the supervision of David Lewis and Gilbert Harman, he wrote a thesis with the wonderful title The Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Truth About Morality and What to Do About It, arguing that:

the enemy, the wolf in sheep’s clothing, is moral realism. Conflicts of interest may be inevitable, but they need not be exacerbated by people’s unflagging confidence that they’re right and that their opponents are wrong.

But why do philosophers cling to moral realism? The answer is simple.

Philosophers, much like the common science denier, love their intuitions. Where science conflicts with common sense it is science that looks suspect. So much so that philosophers have historically continuously embarrassed themselves by defending prejudices, myths, and a great many blunders that we now look upon in shame — and make the hostility of many scientists against philosophy hardly unjustified.

Whereas scientists teach their students that intuitions are unreliable garbage when it comes to understanding the world, many philosophers venerate their intuitions. Those that don’t are naturalists, as I’ve argued in my most popular blog posts here.

And no intuition is stronger in people than the strong conviction that their own deeply held values are the objectively right ones. They are not just a reflection of one’s idiosyncratic set of subjective likes and dislikes, but they are projected upon the world, with the kind of zealotry glee that turns some people into defenders of the poor and others into mass murderers.

But how would we even live in a world that ‘abandons’ morality? Greene and I hold the same view:

The solution […] is to get rid of realist thinking and to start by getting rid of realist language. Speak only in terms that make the subjective nature of value plain.

Some philosophers try to trap you in a kind of gotcha! Hah! You can’t hold values unless you’re a moral realist. But that view is obviously ridiculous. My subjective evaluation of chocolate ice cream over vanilla requires no metaphysical hocus pocus. Nor does my high regard for other animals.

Instead of saying that capital punishment is wrong say that you are opposed to it. Say that it is an ineffective deterrent, difficult to implement in a colorblind fashion, and likely to lead to irreversible mistakes. And then say no more. Instead of saying that eating animals is wrong and a form of murder, say that you are opposed to eating animals because you wish to alleviate suffering and you believe that this practice causes much unnecessary suffering.

It is, of course, strategically tempting to use the archaic language of moral realism to realize one’s preferred vision of the world. If you can convince people that factory farms are objectively wrong, it stands to reason that they’ll have no choice but to become vegans.

Alas, how successful is this approach really?

People hate being moralized at. Not just about veganism. People hate being told that their behaviour, whatever it is, is immoral. Yet, the same people love a good scolding, if they can dish it out to others, who do not act in alignment with their preferred values.

It’s only the belief that we are on the right side of history, that the other side is blinded, and only has to be shown the light, that it seems like such a promising strategy.

Just like the religious zealots standing in town squares with annoying loud speakers in the firm conviction that they’ll be able to pull the wool off your eyes to make you see.

This is why I’ve argued that effective altruists promoting animal welfare, and everyone else for that matter, would be better served becoming a moral nihilist to realize their vision of the world.

And yet, I have little hope that moral realism will land in the dustbin of history. Our minds are just too hard-wired for dogmatism. If people don’t believe scientific results if they don’t align with their intuitions about reality or if they conflict with their values, what hope is there that our species can overcome the plight of moral realism?

item.title: Air Pollution Doesn't Just Dull Minds. It Dulls Teams
item.description:
Teamwork

Air Pollution Doesn't Just Dull Minds. It Dulls Teams

A recent study finds dirty air slows down teams solving problems together.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Teams in polluted air took longer to solve collaborative puzzles.
  • Carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide harmed teams even below WHO safety guidelines.
  • Nitrogen dioxide and fine particles only mattered well above WHO guideline levels.
  • The effect was strongest for corporate teams, those most representative of modern workplaces.

Picture a locked room, a countdown clock, and a group of strangers who must combine clues, argue over theories, and assign tasks fast enough to escape before time runs out. It is a strange setting for psychological research. It is also, as it turns out, an excellent one.

A study published in the Journal of Economic Psychology used data from over 15,000 live escape-room games at a single London venue, played between 2018 and 2022, to ask a simple question: Does air pollution make teams worse at working together? The surprising answer is yes, and the effect is not small.

We already knew pollution could dull individual minds. In one striking study, researchers tracked professional chess players across tournaments and found that a rise in indoor fine particulate matter increased a player's odds of making a costly error, with the effect growing worse as the clock ran down. These were elite players, trained for years to think clearly under pressure, and even they were not immune. Related research has found similar penalties for pollution in call centers, courtrooms, and fruit-packing lines. For example, Sarmiento (2022) analyzed thousands of court hearings across Mexican courthouses and found that a 10-unit increase in particulate matter made hearings run 6.7% longer. Extrapolated across the sample, the pollution effect cost roughly 56 additional working days over the three years studied, time lost not to laziness or incompetence, but to dirtier air on the day of the hearing.

Air Pollution and Team Performance

What had not been tested, until now, is what happens to a group. On high-pollution days, escape-room teams took up to 5% longer, roughly three minutes, to complete a sequence of non-routine, collaborative tasks. The effect was strongest in the larger teams of five or six. The authors then re-ran the analysis for the teams that came for corporate team-building sessions rather than birthday parties, the groups that most resemble how adults actually work together (over 3,000 teams). The effect not only held up, it was actually slightly larger.

The effect also split in an unexpected way across pollutants. Carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide harmed team performance at concentrations already well below the World Health Organization's air quality guidelines. This is worrying: It means that air that counts as officially safe was still problematic enough to slow teams down. On the other hand, nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter only hurt performance once concentrations rose substantially above WHO guideline levels. Those levels are rare in London, but might be common in polluted cities elsewhere.

This is not simply the chess-player story scaled up. Most research on air quality and cognition looks at one person solving one problem. The newer study looked at people coordinating with each other, thinking together, under time pressure. That distinction is the most interesting part of the finding. The researchers also looked at teams made up of people under 16, mostly there for birthday parties, and found no significant pollution effect on their performance, perhaps because the relevant “thinking together” skills are not yet really developed at that age. Younger, informal groups are the least representative of a modern workplace, where success depends on structured collaboration between adults under institutional pressure. The fact that pollution hurt the corporate-style teams but not the youth groups points to something beyond individual fog. It suggests dirty air degrades the coordination itself: the communication, delegation, and shared reasoning that make a team more capable than any one of its members.

Why Does Pollution Dull Teams?

One possible reason for the results is purely physiological. Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen flow to the brain (and might actually kill you because of that, at high concentrations). This blunts reasoning abilities and the kind of creative problem-solving abilities that escape rooms require. No mystery there.

There is, however, another possible channel, which is more psychological and far less clear at the moment. Some research suggests that pollution worsens mood, and a worse mood can make people less cooperative and even more risk-averse. Both of those could slow down a team trying to solve a puzzle together.

Pollution, Economics, and You

That is a bigger deal than it sounds. Escape rooms stand in for many modern-work tasks, from product design to scientific discovery, which are analytical, collaborative, and creative. If pollution taxes the skill set that innovation runs on, air quality becomes an economic variable, not just a health one. Many low- and middle-income countries face far higher pollution levels than London ever reaches, and many are trying to build the exact kind of service-sector, team-based innovation economy that pollution might be undermining. Reducing air pollution, then, might be more than a public health measure. It may be a growth strategy.

A word of caution, though. As always with scientific research, one study, however well designed, is a data point, not a verdict. This study, though, joins a growing body of research linking environmental conditions to cognitive and behavioural outcomes, including work on heat and decision-making previously covered in this space (heat hinders our thinking, can make us violent, and leads to traffic accidents). The pattern is becoming familiar: Our thinking, and our ability to work with others, depends more on our environment than we like to believe.

There is a practical takeaway worth taking seriously if you work in a team, or if you manage one. Air quality is not just a comfort issue for the office. If you have any control over indoor air, in a meeting room, a workshop venue, or a shared lab space, treat ventilation and filtration as tools for better collaboration, not just as amenities. You cannot escape a bad room by thinking harder. Sometimes you just need better air.

item.title: Let There Be Gas Light
item.description:
Gaslighting

Let There Be Gas Light

Examining the origins of gaslighting.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Gaslighting feels like a new problem, but it has been studied for decades.
  • The way psychologists originally used the term gaslighting is quite different from today.
  • Changes to how we think of gaslighting are related to changes in how mental health problems are treated.
  • This older version of gaslighting still occasionally occurs.

Today, the term "gaslighting" is usually used to describe a pattern of psychological abuse where the gaslighter manipulates a target into doubting their own sense of reality. Over the last 10 years, gaslighting has caught the attention of psychologists and the public alike. What most people don't know is that the term gaslighting has been around for much longer than 10 years, and its meaning has changed a great deal in that time.

The etymology of gaslighting as a term for psychological abuse can be traced back to a play written in 1938 by Patrick Hamilton. Lovers of old movies and students of gaslighting are probably familiar with the 1944 Hollywood adaptation of the play, Gaslight, starring Ingrid Bergman and Charles Boyer, and released by MGM. Less familiar, even to modern-day experts on gaslighting, is the earlier British film adaptation of Hamilton's play, released in 1940 and directed by Thorold Dickinson.

The play, and both film adaptations, have more in common than not. All three take place in 1880s London, and feature an adulterous husband who connivingly convinces his wife that she is delusional, and repeatedly threatens her with institutionalization in a psychiatric hospital. In the meantime, he openly flirts with their maid, and sneaks out at night to rummage through the blocked-off attic of the couple's home. He suspects there are tremendously valuable jewels hidden in the attic that belonged to the home's previous owner, whom he murdered decades earlier.

While searching for these jewels, he turns on the attic's gaslights, causing the lighting in the rest of the house to flicker. A common point of confusion is that he adjusts the lights to convince his wife that she is hallucinating. But the flickering is actually an unintended by-product of his search for the jewels and leads his wife to the insight that someone is in the attic and helps break the spell of her husband's abuse.

Gas sconce lights, much like those that revealed the abuse in Gaslight (1944)
Source: Chris F / Pexels

Both the 1944 MGM film and the 1940 British version feature a detective who helps expose the manipulative husband and end his wife's torment, but there is an important difference in the detectives' portrayal. In the British version, the detective is played by Frank Pettingell, who is somewhat portly, fatherly, and not your usual Hollywood heartthrob. Whereas, in the now-classic 1944 version, the detective is played by a young, tall, broad-shouldered, chisel-jawed Joseph Cotton. Unfortunately, the handsome detective can't help but land a kiss on the woman who has, mere minutes earlier, escaped an incredibly dangerous and psychologically abusive marriage. I think most psychologists would agree that she could use at least a night off dating.

The reason for the British film's relative obscurity is that, when MGM purchased the rights to remake it, they demanded that all physical copies of the previous movie be destroyed. I wonder – did the executives responsible for this decision ever contemplate the hypocrisy of trying to gaslight the public about the existence of the original film?

Despite MGM's efforts, the 1940 film survives. Furthermore, it is quite likely that the 1940 film, rather than the more popular 1944 film, is responsible for the modern usage of the term gaslighting, as it was psychiatrists in the United Kingdom, not America, that first used the term clinically. These psychiatrists fixated on the plot point of institutionalization in a psychiatric hospital, not the aspect of the story that is more familiar today, namely, trying to manipulate someone into doubting their own sanity.

The first use of the term gaslighting as a clinical term was in 1969, in the Lancet. Barton and Whitehead described three cases of manipulative attempts to have someone institutionalized on false pretenses. The first case was a middle-aged mechanic, whose wife of 10 years insisted that he was irritable, violent, and his memory was failing. He was kept in the hospital for 12 days but released when no symptoms of mental illness were observed. Upon his release, his wife insisted that his symptoms had worsened and he "belonged in a mental hospital". In the meantime, the man's employer had seen his wife, and her alleged affair partner, discussing their plan to elope once her husband was compulsorily institutionalized.

The second case is quite similar; this time, the false accusations were of excessive alcoholism, and the goal was to take over a family business. The final case study involved workers in a care home for the elderly, who falsely accused a resident of having severe dementia in order to free up her room.

While this is the first time gaslighting was used as a verb to describe attempts to have someone institutionalized in a psychiatric hospital on false pretenses, Barton and Whitehead point out that concerns about this issue can be dated back to at least 1763 in Great Britain.

Today, compared to 1763, 1940, and 1969, the mental health establishment has moved away from compulsory admission to psychiatric hospitals. Furthermore, a period of deinstitutionalization has led to the closure of many of the psychiatric hospitals that would have loomed over targets of gaslighting in the past. Just as our approach to mental health has changed over the years, so has the usage of the term gaslighting.

Today, the focus has shifted to a different element of Hamilton's plot, namely, the attempt to convince someone that they are delusional when they aren't. But this older form of gaslighting, where it is a doctor who is being convinced of the target's mental instability, does still occur on occasion. For example, in 2015, the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine published a case study where a man's new romantic partner was insisting that he had a habit of talking about disturbing and vulgar sexual activity while he was asleep. His partner had used this sleep-talking to "negotiate more favorable domestic financial arrangements for herself", but when the man subtly introduced an audio-recording device into their bedroom, it became apparent that his alleged sleep-talking was fictitious.

item.title: Stop Looking for Someone to Make You Laugh
item.description:
Relationships

Stop Looking for Someone to Make You Laugh

The difference between sharing joy with a partner and outsourcing it to one.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • "Make me laugh" casts a partner as performer and yourself as audience—a consumption model of joy.
  • Research shows shared laughter, not delivered laughter, predicts relationship satisfaction.
  • Happiness depends heavily on intentional activity—a responsibility no partner can carry for you.
  • The fix is one word: Seek someone you laugh with, not someone who makes you laugh.

Scroll through any dating app and one wish appears more than almost any other: "You should make me laugh."

It sounds harmless—charming, even. Who doesn't want laughter in a relationship? But listen closely to the grammar. You should make me laugh. One person performs; the other receives. One is the comedian; the other is the audience. Before the first date has even happened, the job description assigns your future partner a role: supplier of your good moods.

The wish for laughter is healthy. The outsourcing hidden inside it is not.

What the Research Actually Says About Laughter and Love

Laughter genuinely matters in romantic relationships—but not in the way the dating-profile phrase implies. In a study of couples, Kurtz and Algoe (2015) found that the amount of time partners spent laughing together predicted relationship quality and feelings of closeness. It was the shared moment—two nervous systems in sync—that carried the benefit.

A meta-analysis of 39 studies reached the same conclusion from another direction: Hall (2017) found that relationship satisfaction was linked to humor that partners create and appreciate jointly—inside jokes, playful exchanges—rather than to either partner's individual funniness. Being a comedy talent, it turns out, is not what predicts a happy couple. Laughing at the same things is.

In other words: The research supports wanting laughter in your relationship. It does not support hiring someone to produce it for you.

The Problem With Outsourcing Your Mood

"Make me laugh" is a small example of a larger pattern psychologists have been tracking for years: the tendency to hand a romantic partner responsibility for regulating our emotional lives.

Finkel and colleagues (2014) describe how modern partnership has absorbed roles once spread across an entire community—best friend, therapist, entertainer, motivational coach. They argue that expecting one person to meet needs at every level, without investing correspondingly more in the relationship, leaves many couples "suffocating." It asks more of marriage than most marriages can deliver.

The happiness research adds a second problem. A substantial share of our day-to-day happiness is governed by intentional activity—what we choose to do, notice, and cultivate—rather than by our circumstances, including who we're dating (Lyubomirsky, Sheldon, & Schkade, 2005). Self-determination theory reaches a similar verdict: Well-being rests on needs such as autonomy and competence that, by definition, no one can satisfy on your behalf (Deci & Ryan, 2000).

If your baseline joy is a job you've assigned to someone else, two things follow. You have made your happiness contingent on another person's daily performance. And you have handed them a task at which they are guaranteed, eventually, to fail—because no partner is funny on demand, forever, at the end of their own hard days.

The Audience Problem

There is also a quieter cost. An audience evaluates. When your partner's role is to entertain you, their off days become disappointments, and your attention shifts from being with them to reviewing them. Few things are less romantic than a performance review.

And consider the position it puts the other person in. They fell in love; they did not audition. A relationship in which one person is responsible for the weather and the other merely reports on it is not a partnership. It is a service arrangement with affection attached.

The One-Word Fix

None of this means you should delete laughter from your wish list. It means changing one word.

Not: someone who makes me laugh. Instead: someone I laugh with.

The revision looks cosmetic. It is structural. "With" turns joy from something delivered into something co-created. It matches what the research finds actually predicts satisfaction—shared humor, mutual play. And it changes what you look for on those first dates: not "Is this person entertaining me?" but "Do we find the same things funny? Is something light and playful happening between us?"

That second question, incidentally, is far better at detecting compatibility. Plenty of people can be charming for an evening. Whether laughter arises between you is much harder to fake.

Govern Your Own Weather First

The deeper preparation for partnership, then, is not finding a funnier candidate. It is becoming a person whose baseline contentment is self-governed: cultivating your own sources of amusement, play, and meaning, so that a partner's humor is a gift you enjoy rather than a supply you depend on.

People who arrive at a relationship already in decent emotional weather have more to offer and less to demand. They can be delighted by a partner without being dependent on one. And—the pleasant irony—they tend to laugh more with their partners, because shared laughter flourishes precisely where nobody is under pressure to produce it.

So keep laughter on the list. Just rewrite the item. You are not casting a comedian. You are looking for someone to sit beside while the two of you find the world funny together.
